content:
For years, websites were built to do a few simple things well: explain the business, rank in Google and generate leads.

That model still works, but the internet is changing quickly.

We are now moving away from traditional WordPress-based websites and toward AI Managed websites that are faster, more flexible and much easier to adapt as AI changes the way people search, browse and interact with businesses online.

WordPress has been the workhorse of the internet for a long time, and it is not going anywhere overnight. But it was built for a different era of the web. As more AI tools, search engines and automated agents become part of the online experience, we want websites that give us much more control over what is happening behind the scenes.

A Website Should Do More Than Sit There

A modern website should not just wait for someone to visit it.

It should help us understand what visitors are doing, where they came from, which pages are performing well and which parts of the website are actually generating leads.

That is a big part of what we mean by an AI Managed website.

Instead of relying entirely on separate systems like Google Analytics, Google Search Console and Google Ads, we can connect those systems more closely with the website itself and make the information much easier to understand.

Rather than digging through several dashboards, we want to be able to ask simple questions like:

  • Which pages are bringing in the most leads?
  • Which services are getting traffic but not converting?
  • Which pages are losing visibility in search?
  • What should we work on next?

That is where AI becomes genuinely useful. It is not there just to create content or add a chatbot. It can help us understand the website and make better decisions about how to improve it.

AI Search Is Changing SEO

SEO is also changing.

Google still matters, but people are increasingly using tools like ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants to research companies, compare services and get recommendations.

That means we also have to think about Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) and how easily AI systems can understand a website.

This is where having more control over the website becomes extremely important.

Imagine a 50-page website where a new piece of code or structured information suddenly needs to be added so AI crawlers can better understand the content.

On a traditional site, that could mean opening page after page and making the same change over and over again.

With a properly built AI Managed website, we can often make that change once and apply it across the entire site.

That can save hours of work and, more importantly, allows the website to adapt much faster when search technology changes.

AI Can Take a Lot of the Manual Work Out of SEO

The larger a website becomes, the harder it is to manage SEO manually.

Internal linking is a good example.

If a website has dozens of service pages and hundreds of articles, there may be hundreds or even thousands of opportunities to connect related content together.

Doing that by hand takes time.

An AI Managed website can help us understand how all of that content relates, where links are missing and which important pages could use more support.

The same applies to technical SEO, structured data and content updates.

Instead of treating every page as a separate task, we can look at the website as one connected system.

That makes it much easier to improve the site over time without adding hours of repetitive work every month.

The Website Can Become Easier to Understand and Manage

One of the biggest frustrations we see is that business owners often have no simple way to tell whether their website is actually working.

They may have Google Analytics, Google Ads, Search Console, form notifications and other tools, but all of that information is scattered across different platforms.

An AI Managed website gives us the opportunity to bring the most important information together.

  • Traffic
  • Leads
  • Phone clicks
  • Form submissions
  • Search performance
  • Popular pages
  • Conversion activity

More importantly, AI can help explain what those numbers actually mean.

Knowing that traffic increased is useful.

Knowing that traffic increased but leads went down is much more useful.

Knowing which pages caused that change is better still.

That is the type of information we want the website to help surface.

Why We Are Moving Away From Traditional WordPress Builds

WordPress is still a good platform for many websites, but it can become limiting when a business wants deeper integrations, more automation and faster technical changes.

A typical WordPress site often grows by adding another plugin every time a new feature is needed.

  • SEO plugin
  • Analytics plugin
  • Accessibility plugin
  • Caching plugin
  • Form plugin
  • Security plugin
  • Chat plugin

Eventually, a lot of different systems are all trying to work together.

With an AI Managed website, we can build more of those capabilities directly into the platform and control how everything works together.

That gives us more flexibility, better performance and the ability to react much faster when something changes.

If a new AI crawler appears, we can adapt.

If search engines change what they want to see, we can update the site.

If we want to introduce smarter conversion tracking, we can build it in.

If we want an AI assistant to work directly with website data, we can make that possible.

That is the idea behind connecting large language models to a website through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Instead of the AI guessing from a copied report, it can talk to the systems that actually run the site.

The real advantage is not any one feature.

It is having a website that can change as quickly as the internet does.

Is It Time to Consider an AI Managed Website?

A website should not feel outdated the moment a new technology comes along.

It should be built to evolve.

That is why Leanne Digital is moving toward AI Managed websites that give us greater control over SEO, AEO, analytics, conversion tracking, accessibility and future AI integrations without being tied down by the limitations of a traditional website platform.

If your current website is slow to update, difficult to manage or heavily dependent on plugins just to keep up, it may be worth thinking about what the next version of your website should look like.

An AI Managed website is not about adding AI because it is trendy. It is about building a faster, smarter and more adaptable foundation for where the web is going next.

If you are planning a new website or thinking about replacing an older WordPress site, this is the direction we believe is worth considering.

content:
A Pattern I’ve Noticed Over the Years

As the CTO and lead developer for Leanne Digital, I spend a lot of my day investigating issues that get sent my way, usually involving website integration issues, plugin conflicts, or custom code that isn’t behaving the way it should.

A big part of that is inspecting PHP and Javascript code and logs to figure out why things are conflicting and what’s causing problems behind the scenes.

And one pattern I’ve noticed over the years…

A lot of these issues trace back to work that was outsourced through freelancer platforms like Fiverr or Upwork.

Now, to be clear, these platforms aren’t inherently bad. There are talented people on them, and they can be incredibly useful in the right situations.

But there are some risks that business owners don’t always see upfront.

Why Businesses Turn to Freelancer Platforms

It makes sense.

  • Lower cost
  • Quick turnaround
  • Easy access to global talent

If you’re running a business and trying to manage costs, it can feel like a smart move.

I’ve done it myself when I was starting out. When you’re wearing multiple hats, sometimes you just need extra hands to get things done.

Where Things Can Get Tricky

When tasks are simple, everything usually runs smoothly. But once you get into more complex work like custom WordPress functionality, WooCommerce logic, or debugging, communication becomes a big factor.

It’s not just about speaking the same language, it’s about being able to clearly explain issues, understand requirements, and work through problems together. When that part isn’t solid, even small misunderstandings can lead to bigger issues down the line. Sometimes the time it takes to explain the issue takes longer than fixing the issue yourself.

Another thing to keep in mind is how these platforms operate. Many freelancers are working across multiple projects at once, which is completely understandable. But it can sometimes lead to delays or rushed work especially when timelines are tight. In some cases, the immediate problem gets fixed, but the long-term impact isn’t fully considered.

You’ll also often see freelancers listing a wide range of skills and multiple programming languages, frameworks, and platforms. While versatility is valuable, real depth usually comes from specialization. When you’re dealing with something more involved, like a WordPress or WooCommerce setup, having someone who truly knows that ecosystem can make a noticeable difference.

A Real-World Example

I was brought in to look at a WooCommerce site that had started crashing intermittently.

This was a busy eCommerce business doing thousands of dollars per week, and when the site went down, it directly impacted sales.

After digging into it, I learned that some custom code had been added previously to handle a specific shipping scenario.

The developer who wrote it was no longer available, and there wasn’t much documentation.

After working through the site and isolating different components, I eventually found the issue, a small piece of custom code that was causing server errors under certain conditions.

Once it was fixed, the site stabilized.

But the business had already experienced downtime and lost revenue in the process.

It’s Not Just About Cost — It’s About Value

As one industry perspective puts it, low-cost services can sometimes act as a temporary fix rather than a long-term solution, especially when there isn’t a deeper understanding of the business or system behind the work.

When you hire experienced developers or designers, you’re not just paying for the task, you’re paying for:

  • Problem-solving ability
  • Long-term thinking
  • Maintainable, scalable work
  • Ongoing support

When Freelancer Platforms Make Sense

There are definitely good use cases.

Repetitive and Low-Risk Tasks

If the work is simple and repeatable, these platforms are a great fit. Things like data entry, formatting, product uploads, or basic edits can be handled quickly without much risk. You save time and free yourself up for higher value work.

Small Front-End Development Tasks

For minor visual updates or layout tweaks, freelancers can work well. Just make sure to review their portfolio and start with a small task first. If they follow instructions well and the quality is there, you can continue from there with confidence.

Graphic Design and Creative Work

There are some very talented designers on these platforms. If you need a logo, social graphics, or quick design work, you can find good options. Always review past work, check ratings, and make sure the designs are original.

Overflow Work When You’re Busy

If you’re overloaded and need extra hands, these platforms can help you keep things moving. This works best when you already understand the task clearly and can give solid direction. Think of it as support, not full ownership.

Want It Done Right the First Time?

If you’re looking for reliable, high-quality work in SEO, design, WordPress development, and websites that are built to perform and convert…

Contact Leanne Digital today for an honest quote.

FAQ

Is Fiverr or Upwork bad for business?
Not at all. They’re great tools when used correctly. The key is knowing when a task is simple enough to outsource versus when it requires deeper expertise.

Can you build a full WordPress site using a freelancer?
You can, but it comes with risk. Without proper planning, documentation, and long-term support, you may run into issues later — especially as your site grows.

Why are freelancer prices so low?
Many freelancers operate on volume, taking on multiple projects at once. Lower pricing can also reflect differences in experience, specialization, or scope of work.

What should I look for when hiring a freelancer?
Look for a strong portfolio, consistent reviews, clear communication, and ideally start with a small test task before committing to a larger project.

Is it more expensive to fix issues later?
In many cases, yes. Troubleshooting and repairing existing work can take more time than building something properly from the start.

Final Thoughts

Freelancer platforms like Fiverr and Upwork have their place, and when used the right way, they can be a valuable resource.

But when it comes to the core parts of your business, your website, your systems, and anything tied directly to revenue, it’s worth thinking beyond just the upfront cost.

Because in the long run, quality, reliability, and accountability tend to matter a lot more than saving a few dollars at the beginning.

content:
Design for Humans. Structure for Google. Build with Purpose.

After more than 10 years in design and building strategic WordPress websites for service-based businesses, I’ve learned something important:

A beautiful website that lacks clarity will not convert.
A strategic website that lacks personality will not connect.

The magic happens when both work together.

Here’s exactly how I approach every website project.

Step 1: Choose the Audience First

Before design. Before colors. Before images.

We start with people.

Ask yourself:

  • Who is this for?
  • What stage are they at?
  • What problem are they trying to solve?
  • What tone will make them feel understood?

Design is not about what you like. It’s about what makes your audience feel confident enough to take the next step.

If we don’t know who we’re speaking to, everything else becomes guesswork.

Audience clarity drives messaging, structure, visual tone, and conversion strategy. When the audience is clear, decisions become simple.

Step 2: Write the Copy Before You Design

This is where most people get it backwards. They start with colors, or layout, or inspiration screenshots.

But clarity comes first.

Every page must answer five things:

  1. What is this page about?
  2. Who does it help?
  3. What does it help them with?
  4. What result do they get?
  5. What are the next steps?

If the copy isn’t clear, the design will feel off. No amount of styling can fix confusing messaging.

Clarity first. Styling second.

Step 3: One Page = One Topic (SEO Foundation)

This is the structure-for-Google part.

Every page has one job: one main topic, one focus keyword, one clear intent. No mixing services. No vague headlines.

Your H1 must include the focus keyword. For example:

Instead of “Transforming Outdoor Spaces” — write “Residential Rubber Surfacing in Fort Myers.”

Specific beats clever.

When each page focuses on a single topic, Google understands it, visitors understand it, and your authority increases. Simple structure wins.

Step 4: Structure the Page with Headings

Headings create your layout automatically.

  • H1 = What this page is about
  • H2s = The main sections that explain it

Each H2 becomes a section on the page. This creates logical flow, easy scanning, SEO alignment, and a natural wireframe. Your layout has direction before you ever design a single section.

Step 5: Layout your copy

Now we organize. Not design — organize.

Stack your sections vertically:

  • Hero (H1 + short supporting text + CTA)
  • Trust
  • Services or explanation
  • Proof
  • Clear call to action

If something feels messy at this stage, it’s almost always a copy issue. Fix the messaging before adjusting the layout. Structure removes overwhelm.

Step 6: Decide the Vibe (Look & Feel)

Now we move into visual language. Based on your audience, ask: is the vibe calm, corporate, playful, bold, luxurious, or grounded?

The vibe guides typography, color palette, image style, and icon style. Design decisions must match the emotional tone your audience expects. If you’re serving executives, the vibe is different than if you’re serving new moms or creatives.

The visual system should reinforce the message, not compete with it.

Step 7: Choose Typography

Typography is structure, not decoration. Keep it simple: one headline font, one body font.

For the main headline, choose something with personality — a little more expressive. This is where the vibe shows up. But your body copy should stay simple.

Larger fonts are easier to read, which gives you more flexibility to use a slightly expressive typeface for big headlines. Body text is smaller, so readability matters more than style. Your body font should be clean, easy on the eyes, and highly legible at smaller sizes.

Make sure your typography has strong contrast, supports clear hierarchy, and feels consistent across the page. When hierarchy is strong, users don’t feel lost — they feel guided.

Step 8: Build Color Rhythm

Color should create flow, not chaos. Avoid pure white and pure black — they can feel harsh.

Instead, use very subtle background colors (almost white), alternating section tones to divide content, and darker background sections for emphasis. Each section should feel visually separated.

Typography must always have enough contrast to read easily. If people can’t comfortably read your content, they won’t stay.

Step 9: Add Images and Icons for Skimmability

Images and icons are not filler. They should support the message, clarify ideas, break up heavy text, and improve scanning.

Your website is not a novel. People skim before they commit. Visual elements reinforce understanding and reduce cognitive load.

Step 10: Final Check

Before launch, I ask:

  • Can I understand what this page is about in 5 seconds?
  • Is there only one main topic?
  • Is the next step obvious?
  • Is it readable?
  • Does the design match the audience?

If the answer is yes, it works.

Why This Process Works

This process balances human psychology, clear communication, SEO structure, and intentional design. It removes overwhelm, removes guesswork, and removes trendy-but-confusing layouts.

It builds websites that build trust, rank strategically, guide users naturally, and convert with clarity.

Design for humans.
Structure for Google.
Build with purpose.

You got this. And if you don’t, I’m only a contact form away 😉

content:
• Key Takeaways
    Amazon is not a flexible storefront — it’s a rigid, rule-based system where many decisions are permanent and mistakes compound over time.
  • Testing and “figuring it out as you go” can backfire on Amazon. Even deleted products can leave behind conflicts that are difficult to undo.
  • GTINs (Global Trade Item Numbers) identify real, physical products and are permanent once used. SKUs are internal tools — confusing the two is a common and costly mistake.
  • Product structure must be planned before anything is created. Parents must exist before children, and incorrect variation trees are one of the biggest pitfalls for new sellers.
  • Amazon prioritizes compliance over creativity. White-background primary images, structured copy, and strict formatting rules are not optional.
  • Changes on Amazon are slow and inconsistent. Edits may take hours or days to appear, and repeated changes can make problems worse, not better.
  • Details like product weight, dimensions, and packaging are critical backend data points — not minor fields — and incorrect values can affect eligibility, fees, and stability.
  • Amazon rewards patience, structure, and precision. Sellers who rush or assume flexibility often end up rebuilding their listings from scratch.

Taming the mighty Amazon is not easy. It’s one of the most powerful e-commerce platforms on the planet, but it’s also one of the most rigid, unforgiving, and unintuitive systems you’ll ever work with. Amazon does not encourage experimentation, it does not reward improvisation, and it rarely explains why something isn’t working.

If you’re thinking about selling on Amazon, this article is meant to give you a realistic picture of what’s involved — not the polished success stories, but the actual process. Amazon can absolutely work for your business, but only if you approach it with structure, patience, and a clear understanding of its limitations.

Step 1: Understand That Amazon Is a System, Not a Storefront

Most people come to Amazon expecting it to behave like Shopify or WooCommerce — flexible, visual, and forgiving. Amazon is none of those things. It operates more like a massive rule-based system layered on top of aging infrastructure. Some parts of the interface look modern, but behind the scenes, many tools are antiquated, slow, and surprisingly fragile.

Edits don’t always save. Pages crash. Fields appear editable but aren’t. Changes can take hours — sometimes days — to appear across Amazon’s systems. And when something goes wrong, the platform rarely tells you what the problem is, only that there is one.

One of the clearest examples of this came early on when we set up a series of test products to understand how Amazon handled variations and identifiers. Everything looked correct on the surface, but once the products were submitted, we discovered that Amazon had permanently tied our paid GTINS to these test products — even after they were deleted. What was meant to be a harmless test ended up creating conflicts that had to be carefully untangled later.

That experience taught a critical lesson: Amazon remembers everything, and you don’t get unlimited do-overs.

Step 2: Learn the Language Early (GTINs and SKUs Matter More Than You Think)

Two acronyms show up everywhere on Amazon, and misunderstanding them causes more problems than almost anything else: GTIN and SKU.

A GTIN stands for Global Trade Item Number. It’s the barcode number that identifies a specific physical product anywhere in the world. Amazon checks GTINs against the official GS1 database to confirm that:

  • The product exists
  • The brand matches exactly
  • The GTIN hasn’t been reused improperly

Amazon treats GTINs as permanent. Once a GTIN is used, Amazon associates it with an internal ASIN (their product ID), and that relationship doesn’t disappear just because you delete a listing. This is where many sellers get stuck — especially if they experiment, reuse GTINs, or try to “clean things up later.”

A SKU, on the other hand, is your internal identifier. It’s how you track products inside Seller Central. SKUs are flexible and can be changed or replaced, but GTINs are not. Confusing the two leads sellers to believe they have more freedom than they actually do.

The key takeaway here is simple:
GTINs identify the physical product. SKUs organize it internally. One is permanent, the other is not.

Step 3: Plan the Entire Product Structure Before Creating Anything

This is one of the biggest pitfalls for new Amazon sellers: jumping straight into creating products without designing the structure first.

Amazon uses a parent–child product model, and it is extremely strict about it. Parent products are non-buyable placeholders used only to group variations. Child products are the actual sellable items. The order matters — parents must be created before children — and once a structure is in place, many elements cannot be changed.

This is where things often go wrong:

  • Products are created in the wrong order
  • Variations are grouped incorrectly
  • Parents are treated like real products
  • Sellers assume they can “fix it later”

In reality, fixing it later often means deleting products, rebuilding structures, and dealing with lingering conflicts from Amazon’s memory of what existed before. This is exactly what happened with those early test products — the structure seemed harmless at the time, but it created long-term complications.

Amazon does not like flexibility. It likes clearly defined trees, consistent variation themes, and clean relationships between parents and children. If this step isn’t planned carefully, everything downstream becomes harder.

Step 4: Create Assets the Amazon Way (Not the Creative Way)

Amazon has very specific expectations when it comes to product assets, and creativity takes a back seat to compliance.

For primary images, Amazon expects:

  • A pure white background
  • A clear, front-facing product
  • No text, no badges, no overlays

Secondary images can tell more of a story, but even then, Amazon is strict about claims, consistency, and formatting. Uploading the wrong type of image can delay approvals or suppress listings.

Copy follows the same rules. Product titles, descriptions, and bullet points must be factual, structured, and compliant. Over-marketing, exaggerated claims, or vague language can trigger rejections or silent edits by Amazon’s system.

This is also where Amazon’s delays become very noticeable. You might upload images or edit copy and see nothing change for hours. In some cases, edits apply in one area but not another. Making repeated changes too quickly often makes things worse, not better.

Step 5: Final Details Are Not “Small Details” on Amazon

On most platforms, things like product weight, dimensions, and packaging details feel minor. On Amazon, they are not.

These fields affect:

  • Shipping calculations
  • Storage fees
  • Product eligibility
  • Backend validations

Some of these details can only be reliably edited through inventory files, not the user interface. Others appear editable but get overwritten automatically. Incorrect weights or units can cause listings to behave unpredictably or fail internal checks.

This is one of the last steps, but it’s also one of the most important. Once these values are locked in and accepted, correcting them later can be frustrating and time-consuming.

Final Thoughts — And How We Can Help

Amazon is powerful, but it is not friendly. It rewards structure, patience, and precision — and it punishes guesswork. Many of the problems sellers run into don’t come from doing things “wrong,” but from doing them out of order or without understanding how permanent certain decisions are.

This is exactly why Leanne Digital offers an all-in-one Amazon setup service.

We handle:

  • Designing the correct product structure from the start
  • Creating compliant product assets, including white-background primary images
  • Producing multiple images per product to support conversions
  • Writing Amazon-ready product copy, including titles, descriptions, and bullet points
  • Building the full parent-child product tree correctly (parents first — always)
  • Ensuring product details, weights, and units are filled in accurately and consistently

Amazon doesn’t leave much room for error. If you’d rather avoid costly missteps, delays, and rebuilds, we can take care of the heavy lifting and set your store up the right way — the first time.

If you’re ready to sell on Amazon without learning every lesson the hard way, Leanne Digital can handle it for you.

description: Learn more about Leanne Digital | Top Indigenous Creatives from Peguis First Nation
excerpt: Key Takeaways Jordan Stranger, Leanne Jones, Diandre Thomas Hart, and Fredrick Spence are leading the way in art, design, and creative storytelling. Designers like Alyssia…
content:
Key Takeaways

  • Jordan Stranger, Leanne Jones, Diandre Thomas Hart, and Fredrick Spence are leading the way in art, design, and creative storytelling.
  • Designers like Alyssia Sutherland are bringing Indigenous fashion to international stages.
  • Joshua Whitehead is amplifying Indigenous stories through award-winning writing.
  • William Prince is sharing the voice of Peguis with the world through music.
  • Spotted Eagle Handmade and other beadwork artists are preserving culture and tradition through their craft.

When I think of Peguis First Nation, I think of my roots. I grew up in Selkirk, the original intended land of Peguis, surrounded by people who shared this deep connection. For many of us, especially those in my generation, this is a time of reclaiming our strength, taking up space, and showing the world the incredible talent that has always been here.

Seeing Indigenous creatives from Peguis First Nation shine on global stages is empowering. Whether it’s fashion in Milan, a JUNO-winning voice, or bold art on gallery walls, it encourages me to do the same. Our voices deserve to be heard.

This list is more than a collection of names. It’s a celebration of storytellers, designers, entrepreneurs, and artists who represent the heart of Peguis.

Indigenous Visual Artists and Designers from Peguis First Nation

Illustrations By Leanne Jones

Growing up, I spent many hours at my Nana’s house. She had Indigenous artwork on the walls painted by my uncle and APTN was always on the TV because another uncle was acting in a show. That connection to family, art, and storytelling shaped how I see the world as a designer.

Jordan Stranger

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Jordan Stranger (@totemdoodem)

Jordan is one of the most recognized Indigenous visual artists from Peguis. His breathtaking pencil crayon work on black paper is deeply emotional and spiritual. I had seen his work for years before realizing he was the artist behind it. As someone who graduated from the same program I did, his success inspires me to take up more space in the creative industry.

View His Work Here

Leanne Jones

I’m proud to be part of this growing wave of Indigenous entrepreneurs in creative industries. Through my company, Leanne Digital, I focus on marketing and branding to help other Indigenous companies and organizations be seen and heard. My work as an Indigenous graphic designer in Canada is about more than design. It’s about visibility, storytelling, and helping others take up space.

Learn More About My Indigenous Graphic Design Services

Diandre Thomas Hart

Diandre is the Executive Director of Buffalo Hyde Creative. Her work in digital media, photography, and videography has taken her to incredible projects, including documenting the Treaty One team’s trip to Milan Fashion Week. She represents Peguis with creative strength and vision.
Learn More About Diandre Thomas Hart

Fredrick Spence

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Fredrick Lyle Spence (@spence_custom_carving)

Fredrick is a talented Indigenous carver and crafter. He works with soapstone, runs healing workshops, and dreams of opening an Indigenous art gallery. His art is more than visual expression. It is community building and cultural preservation.

View His Work Here

Indigenous Fashion Designers from Peguis First Nation

Powwows have always inspired me. The colors of the regalia, the movement, and the feeling of community are unforgettable. That vibrancy often shows up in my design work, and it is the same creative energy I see in these incredible Indigenous fashion designers.

Alyssia Sutherland

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Alyssia Sutherland (@allysribbons)

Alyssia is the designer behind Ally’s Ribbons. She blends traditional ribbon skirt artistry with modern fashion, proudly representing Peguis at Milan Fashion Week. Her work shows how Indigenous fashion can be both rooted and visionary.

View Her Work Here

Indigenous Writers and Storytellers

Joshua Whitehead

Book Cover of Joshua Whitehead book Jonny Appleseed

Joshua is a two-spirit Oji-Cree/nehiyaw author from Peguis and one of the most celebrated Indigenous writers and storytellers in Canada. His novel Jonny Appleseed won Canada Reads 2021 and captured hearts across the country.

Joshua and I went to high school together in Selkirk. Seeing someone from my own community and school make such a powerful impact in the literary world is incredibly meaningful to me. His writing is raw, honest, and full of heart. It proves that incredible stories are growing right here in our own community.

Follow Joshua On Instagram Here

Indigenous Musicians from Peguis First Nation

Music has always been a heartbeat in Peguis. From powwow drums to world tours, we are part of a long line of Indigenous musicians in Canada making waves far beyond home.

William Prince

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by William Prince (@williamprince)

William Prince is a celebrated folk and country musician whose voice carries the stories of Peguis to audiences around the world. His albums Earthly Days, Reliever, and Gospel First Nation have earned national acclaim. His music speaks of love, faith, and land, and it inspires so many of us to stand proud in who we are.

Beyond big names like William, there are countless singers and performers who bring life to community events and powwows every year. They are part of the story too.

Learn More About William Prince Here

Manitoba Beadwork Artists and Traditional Crafters

There are so many Manitoba beadwork artists, seamstresses, and traditional makers in Peguis. Many of them sell their work at local craft markets and online, creating pieces that carry our stories and teachings through every bead, stitch, and pattern. These Indigenous carvers and crafters keep culture alive in such a beautiful and meaningful way.

One of those artists is my cousin, the creator behind Spotted Eagle Handmade
, whose beadwork is bold, intricate, and full of spirit. I also had the privilege of designing her logo, which made the project feel even more special. Seeing her build her business and share her craft with the world fills me with pride.

You can also find incredible work from beadwork artists and crafters at local shops and boutiques such as Teecka Aboriginal Boutique,Winnipeg Trading Post, Dene Cree Designs, and Indigenous Reflections, to name a few. These spaces are helping Indigenous creatives reach wider audiences while keeping traditional craft alive.

If you see a craft table or come across an Indigenous-owned boutique, stop and take a closer look. These are the hands that hold generations of knowledge. Support them, follow them, and help their art continue to thrive.

Celebrating Indigenous Entrepreneurs in Creative Industries

I want people reading this, whether they are from Peguis or beyond, to feel empowered and inspired. We are strong, talented, and resourceful.

The Indigenous creatives from Peguis First Nation featured here are only the beginning. Ten years from now, I can only imagine the artists, designers, and storytellers who will emerge. I hope this list inspires more of us to step forward, take up space, and share our gifts with the world.

title: Web Designer vs. Web Developer: What’s the Difference
description: Learn more about Leanne Digital | Web Designer vs. Web Developer: What’s the Difference
excerpt: Key Takeaways A web design er focuses on what people see and how they experience your website. A web developer focuses on how everything works behind the scenes. The roles often…
content:
Key Takeaways

  • A web designer focuses on what people see and how they experience your website.
  • A web developer focuses on how everything works behind the scenes.
  • The roles often overlap in areas like responsive design, accessibility, and performance.
  • When both skill sets work together, the result is a website that’s both beautiful and functional.
  • Leaning into strengths creates a smoother process, faster timelines, and stronger results.

When I first started designing websites, I tried to do everything myself. I’d design, build, troubleshoot, and fix every little thing behind the scenes. Over time, I realized something really important. The best websites are built through collaboration.

That’s when I started working with Gary, my developer partner. We each bring different strengths to the table. I focus on the design and user experience, and he makes sure everything runs smoothly behind the scenes. This balance has allowed us to create websites that not only look great but work beautifully.

If you’ve ever started a website project, you’ve probably heard the words web designer and web developer used like they mean the same thing. They don’t. But they do work closely together to make websites that not only look beautiful but actually work.

Since this is something I get asked about a lot, I want to break it down in a way that’s easy to understand and give you a little behind-the-scenes look at how me and Gary work together.

What I Do as a Web Designer

My work is all about designing with purpose. I focus on making a website easy to read, easy to navigate, and visually interesting so that my clients’ customers understand their message quickly.

For me, the research phase is where the magic starts. I love looking at other websites, browsing Pinterest, analyzing award-winning sites, and studying competitors. It honestly feels like walking through an art gallery, except I get to turn that inspiration into something real.

I’m a little more technical than the average designer, but I also believe time is valuable. I want to focus on the part I’m best at so my clients get my strongest work. That’s why I collaborate with Gary on the development side. Design after all is what I studied for 4 years in collage at Red River College Polytechnic.

What Gary Does as a Web Developer

One of the most common questions I get asked when I’m working with clients is “Who is Gary”

Gary is the techinal mastermind behind Leanne Digital. He tackles the things most people don’t see but are absolutely critical:

  • Technical integrations and troubleshooting
  • DNS and email issues
  • Website development and migrations
  • Form setups and error fixes

While I focus on what people see, Gary focuses on how everything actually works. It’s a powerful combo.

Where Design and Development Overlap

Here’s the thing. Designers often end up doing a bit of development, and developers often do a bit of design. The roles overlap, especially on things like:

  • Making sure the site looks great on mobile and desktop
  • Speed and performance
  • Accessibility and usability
  • How elements are structured and interact with users

But at the end of the day, designers think about the user’s experience, and developers think about the mechanics that make it all work smoothly.

How It All Started

Our very first project together was Bloc 15. This was our test run as a team.

Before Gary came on board, I was building websites very differently. He showed me how Astra and Elementor could give me more flexibility without limiting my design vision. I showed him how I design in Figma and how we could use it to collaborate seamlessly.

The project went so well that we kept going and eventually built sites like GBT Logistics
and Oatley Vigmond.
.

Why This Designer and Developer Duo Works

What makes our partnership strong is that we lean into our strengths. I can dive deep into design, storytelling, and UX. Gary can build out the technical side and make everything run like clockwork.

When both sides are doing what they’re best at, the results speak for themselves. Faster projects, cleaner builds, and websites that feel effortless for users.

Final Thoughts

If you’re starting a website project, understanding the difference between a designer and a developer can help you make smarter decisions and find the right people for the job.

A designer shapes the vision.
A developer builds the foundation.
Together, they make something powerful.

If you’re ready to bring your website idea to life, let’s chat. I’d love to show you what a good designer and developer team can do.

title: My Favourite Spots in Winnipeg to Work Remotely
description: Learn more about Leanne Digital | My Favourite Spots in Winnipeg to Work Remotely
excerpt: Key Takeaways The Forks is the perfect mix of focus and fun — grab a cinnamon bun, find a seat upstairs, and take a quick arcade break when you need to reset. Starbucks is…
content:
Key Takeaways

  • The Forks is the perfect mix of focus and fun — grab a cinnamon bun, find a seat upstairs, and take a quick arcade break when you need to reset.
  • Starbucks is reliable, social, and great for casual networking — sometimes showing up with your laptop opens unexpected doors.
  • IKEA is a dream for parents — free childcare, strong coffee, and plenty of outlets make it a guilt-free work haven.
  • Scout Coffee is cozy and kid-friendly — ideal when you want to work while your little ones play.
  • Winnipeg has no shortage of creative work spots — you just have to find the one that fits your mood that day.

Working remotely sounds like a dream and it is but when your office is also your home, sometimes the laundry, dishes, and half-eaten snacks on the counter start calling your name louder than your inbox.

I work full-time (actually, more than full-time) running my Graphic Design and Web Design business from home. I’ve got a great home office setup for client meetings, but every once in a while, I need to escape my house, recharge, and get work done somewhere that doesn’t come with chores attached.

When I really want to focus like deep into design work or catching up on emails — I grab my laptop, my charger (outlets are non-negotiable), and head out. Here are a few of my favorite spots in Winnipeg to work remotely.

The Forks

If I had to pick one spot that’s equal parts inspiring and practical, it’s The Forks. I like sitting upstairs in the coworking-style area where students and other professionals work too. It has a great atmosphere, and if you go early enough, you can usually grab a spot with an outlet.

For breakfast, I love getting a London Fog latte and a cinnamon bun from Tall Grass Prairie(if you’re local, you know). When I need a mid-day break, you’ll find me at Phantom Amusement playing StepMania. I’m actually a big DDR fan… I can even play on heavy difficulty. It’s the best kind of brain break and workout rolled into one.

Between the coffee, the river views, and the culture, The Forks always leaves me feeling refreshed and recharged.

Starbucks

Starbucks might not be the most original pick, but it’s definitely reliable and that’s part of the charm. I usually go to the Pembina location, but honestly, they’re all good. It’s one of those places where it just feels normal to pull out your laptop and get to work.

I’ve actually met a few people there just by showing up. My laptop is covered in geeky stickers, which tends to be a conversation starter. Once, someone came up and asked what I was working on turned out they were a startup founder. I handed them my business card, and just like that, a new connection. Another time, I ended up chatting with someone who worked in government about the importance of design and how you can literally track its impact with analytics.

My go-to order is a chai tea latte and a lemon loaf. I always wear headphones, so it’s not really about the noise it’s about the energy. There’s something about being in a place where people are working and talking that feels social, even if you’re in your own little zone.

IKEA

If you’re a mom who works remotely, let me tell you IKEA is a hidden gem.

They’ll watch your kids for an hour and a half for free if you’re an IKEA Family member. There’s literally nowhere else that does that. My kids loves Smaland! There’s a ball pit, coloring, and movies. It’s like a little hideout for them, and I get 90 uninterrupted minutes to work in peace.

I usually grab my laptop, headphones, and some soup or a drink and sit by the window. Sometimes I even sneak in a bit of shopping afterward. I love their office supplies or just walk around to get my steps in. I haven’t met another parent doing the same yet, but honestly, it would be fun to team up with another working mom one day.

Scout: Coffee + Community

Scout Coffee is a mix of cozy and chaotic — in the best way. It’s got good coffee, snacks, and a big play area for kids. It’s not always the easiest place to concentrate (especially if your kids are still little), but it’s perfect if you want to get out of the house without hiring a babysitter.

I usually grab a regular coffee and whatever the special is that day. My kids love the juice boxes and donuts, and there are plenty of toys to keep them entertained.

If your little ones can play independently and you can tune out the background noise, Scout is a win.

Other Winnipeg Work Spots Worth Checking Out

Here are a few other great places around the city where I’ve worked or plan to work soon:

  • CMU
  • The Leaf
  • Thom Bargen (Sherbrook)
  • Public Library
  • Seven
  • Mountain Bean
  • Daily Grind
  • Little Sister (South Osborne)
  • Café Postal
  • VA Café
  • Thom Bargen (Corydon)
  • St. Vital Mall Food Court
  • Lounge @ Silver Heights
  • Kilter
  • Local coworking spaces

Each one has its own vibe — from calm coworking energy to lively café chatter — depending on what kind of focus (or inspiration) you’re craving.

Final Thoughts

Working remotely is amazing, but it’s even better when you find the right environment to match your mood. Whether it’s the creative buzz at The Forks, the social hum of Starbucks, or the glorious childcare hack that is IKEA, Winnipeg has plenty of spots that make working remotely feel a little less like “work” and a little more like you time.

title: Why Strategic Graphic and Web Design Matters More Than Ever
description: Learn more about Leanne Digital | Why Strategic Graphic and Web Design Matters More Than Ever
excerpt: Key Takeaways Strategic graphic and web design is more than making things look nice — it is about connecting with your audience, solving their problems, and guiding them toward a…
content:
Key Takeaways

  • Strategic graphic and web design is more than making things look nice — it is about connecting with your audience, solving their problems, and guiding them toward a solution.
  • Trust is the most important currency in today’s business world. Design builds that trust by making people feel seen, understood, and safe.
  • Pretty visuals are everywhere, but connection is what cuts through the noise and makes your brand memorable.
  • Strategic design follows a journey: know your audience, align your brand, set clear goals, use data to guide decisions, and tell a compelling visual story.
  • When design is done with strategy, the results speak for themselves: more leads, stronger customer relationships, and higher conversions.
  • Businesses that focus on authentic connection will not just gain customers — they will gain fans and supporters who cheer them on.

Gone are the days when graphic designers were only asked to create “something that looks nice.” The design industry has shifted, and businesses now expect more from us. And honestly, I’m here for it.

At Leanne Digital, I bring strategic graphic design and web design into every project. Because design is no longer just about pretty visuals. It is about creating authentic connections that build trust, solve real problems, and inspire action.

What is Strategic Graphic Design?

At its core, strategic design means thinking beyond the surface. It is not just design that looks good, but design that works hard for your business.

Strategic graphic and web design always considers three things:

  • The audience: Who are we speaking to, and what do they value?
  • The problem: What challenges or needs does the audience have?
  • The solution: How can your business or organization meet those needs in a way that feels trustworthy and authentic?

The goal isn’t just to wow people. The goal is to create something useful, genuine, and meaningful.

Good Design vs. Strategic Design

Good Design asks questions like:

  • Is the design consistent with the brand’s identity?
  • Can people easily understand and navigate it?
  • Does it catch the eye and look professional?

Strategic Graphic and Web Design goes further:

  • Who is the audience, and what do they care about?
  • What problem are they facing that needs solving?
  • How can visuals, messaging, and layout guide them toward a solution?
  • Does the design build trust and motivate action?

Why Trust Matters

People are cautious, and for good reason. In today’s world, scams and inauthentic marketing are everywhere. Customers want to feel seen, understood, and safe when making a purchase.

When you use design to make people feel directly spoken to, they are far more willing to spend money with you. That trust is everything.

Without it, even the prettiest visuals will not move the needle.

The Problem With “Just Pretty Visuals”

We’re constantly bombarded with ads, templates, and endless “good design” thanks to tools like Canva. Pretty graphics used to stand out. Now they are the default.

Here’s the truth:

  • Pretty visuals alone don’t cut through the noise.
  • People are craving connection, not decoration.
  • Strategic design is what makes a brand memorable.

If you want people to pay attention, your design has to say: “This is for you. We understand you.”

The Process: Designing With Strategy

When I start a design project, I don’t just jump straight into picking colors or fonts. Strategic design is a journey, and it always begins with understanding people.

Step 1: Know Your Audience

Your audience is at the heart of everything. Not just their age or gender, but who they are as people. What do they care about? What kind of vibe are they looking for when they connect with a brand?

When I design, I think about how to appeal to their aspirations. Do they want a brand that feels approachable and community-driven? Or are they looking for something sleek and professional that gives them confidence? The goal is to make them feel like the design was made just for them.

Step 2: Build Brand Alignment and Consistency

Once I know the audience, the next step is making sure your brand shows up in a consistent way across all touchpoints. Your website, social media, and print materials should feel like they belong to the same family.

When your audience sees that consistency, they start to think, “This business always shows up the same way. I know them. I trust them.” That recognition turns into comfort, and comfort turns into loyalty.

Step 3: Set Clear Goals

Design without a purpose is just decoration. That’s why I always ask: what do you need your design to do?

  • Do you want more awareness?
  • Do you want more leads?
  • Do you want more email signups or sales?

Design should guide your audience toward these goals. Maybe it’s through a bold call-to-action, a simplified layout that naturally directs the eye, or a landing page that makes it easy to say “yes.”

Step 4: Let Data Lead the Way

Creativity is essential, but data tells us what actually works. That’s why I look at analytics, research, and SEO insights to guide design choices.

For example, we know that page load speed is more important for SEO than flashy animations. A clean, fast-loading website will outperform a slow, complicated one every time. Data helps us refine the creative work so it not only looks good but also performs.

Step 5: Tell a Story Through Visuals

Finally, this is where everything comes together. Humans are wired for stories, and design is one of the most powerful ways to tell them.

Your customers should feel like they’re the hero of their own story. Your business is the trusted sidekick that helps them succeed.

That’s where visuals come in:

  • Colors set the mood.
  • Typography creates personality.
  • Imagery makes the experience relatable and inspiring.

Together, these elements tell a story that makes your audience feel seen, understood, and connected.

Example: Leanne Digital Rebrand

When I rebranded Leanne Digital, I used strategic design principles to attract the right audience.

My audience: Small businesses and organizations who want personalized support and real human connection. Many have been burned by big agencies and want someone approachable but capable.

My solution:

  • Friendly, rounded fonts and a playful logo (to show approachability).
  • My name as the brand name (to emphasize human connection).
  • Dark blues, purples, and teals (to show professionalism, tech focus, and high-quality design).

The results: After rebranding, my leads doubled because people could see themselves in my brand and trusted me more.

Measuring Success

So how do you know if strategic design is working?

Here are a few signs:

  • More inquiries and leads (because people feel confident reaching out).
  • Longer customer relationships (because trust turns customers into fans).
  • Higher conversion rates (because design is aligned with business goals, not just aesthetics).

My Perspective as a Strategic Designer

What sets me apart is empathy. I’m not just a designer working for businesses, I am right there alongside them.

I understand what it feels like to be a small business owner trying to connect with an audience. That’s why I collaborate closely, listen deeply, and always design from the audience’s perspective.

Advice for Businesses

Here’s the biggest truth:
Your business is not a beauty pageant. It is not about being the most popular or the most beautiful.

It is about creating authentic connections with your audience so you attract quality customers who not only buy from you, but also support you, cheer for you, and tell others about you.

If you looking for a Graphic and Web Designer who truely understand your goals for you business feel free to schedule a call with me today!

content:
Why Website Security Matters More Than Ever

Your website isn’t just a collection of pages on the internet. It’s your brand’s identity, your sales channel, and often the very first impression you make on potential customers. Yet, despite how central it is to business success, website security is often overlooked — until something goes wrong.

Let’s take a closer look at why website security is so important, what can go wrong when it’s ignored, and how to make sure your site stays safe.

What Is Website Security?

Website security is the practice of protecting your site from cyber threats, data breaches, and downtime. At its core, it’s about keeping hackers out, protecting sensitive information, and ensuring your website continues running smoothly for visitors.

A secure website not only keeps your data safe, but also reassures your customers that you take their privacy seriously. It’s what allows them to confidently enter their details, make purchases, or contact you without hesitation.

Think of it as locking the doors to your business at night — it’s not optional, it’s essential.

Understanding Website Security Risks

Just like a house has different points of entry, websites have multiple vulnerabilities that hackers can exploit. Some of the most common risks include:

  • Malware: harmful code that can damage files or steal data.
  • Phishing attacks: scams designed to trick users into handing over sensitive information.
  • DDoS attacks: floods of fake traffic that make your site unavailable.
    Weak passwords or outdated plugins: easy entry points for attackers.

The consequences can be severe — stolen customer information, a damaged reputation, lost sales, and costly downtime.

Why Website Security Is Just as Important as Design

A sleek, modern website design can grab attention. But if your site isn’t secure, design won’t matter for long. Visitors who see “Not Secure” warnings in their browser won’t stick around. Search engines may penalize your site, and word of a breach can spread quickly.

Great design attracts visitors, but great security keeps them there. Without it, even the most beautifully designed site risks being abandoned.

The Hidden Costs of Neglecting Security

It’s easy to assume a website hack is just a technical headache. In reality, the damage can spread far beyond the digital world.

Here’s what neglecting website security could cost you:

  • Reputation: once customers feel their data isn’t safe, trust is difficult to rebuild.
  • Revenue: downtime, blacklisting, and browser warnings all mean fewer sales.
  • Recovery: cleaning up malware and restoring systems is almost always more expensive than prevention.

In short, a breach can hit your business where it hurts most — financially and publicly.

What Does a Website Need to Be Secure?

A truly secure website doesn’t rely on a single fix. It’s built with layers of protection that work together.

Every website should have:

  • SSL certificate to encrypt visitor data.
  • Daily backups so recovery is fast and stress-free.
  • Firewalls and malware scanning to block suspicious activity.
  • Regular updates for plugins, themes, and software.
  • Strong authentication with secure passwords and multi-factor logins.

Think of it as adding locks, alarms, and cameras to your online business — one safeguard is never enough on its own.

Your Role in Website Security

Even with the best tools in place, website security isn’t completely automatic. Business owners play an important role in keeping their sites safe. Some simple best practices include:

  • Using strong, unique passwords.
  • Only installing trusted plugins or themes.
  • Limiting admin access to those who truly need it.
  • Staying on top of updates instead of letting them pile up.

Security is a shared responsibility: technology provides the foundation, but good habits keep it strong.

Protecting Your Website with Ongoing Maintenance

Website security isn’t a one-time project — it’s an ongoing commitment. Just as you maintain your car with oil changes and inspections, your website needs consistent care.

That’s where professional Website Maintenance and Security Packages make a difference. With daily backups, plugin updates, 24/7 monitoring, and malware protection, you can protect your site without the stress of doing it all yourself.

Whether you’re a small business needing essential coverage or an established company looking for advanced performance and priority support, there’s a package to fit your needs.

You can explore the plans here: Website Maintenance & Security Plans

Keeping your site secure means more than avoiding headaches — it means protecting your customers, your reputation, and your business future.

Your home page is kind of like a first date. You want to make a great impression, show off your best qualities, and most importantly make the other person want to see you again (or in this case, click your call-to-action).

When creating your home page, put yourself in your customer’s shoes.
What are they looking for? What questions do they have? What action do you want them to take?

Thinking about their journey will make it so much easier to plan out your content and design.

Every home page is a little different depending on your business, but here’s my go-to layout that works across pretty much every industry:

1. Hero Section

This is your elevator pitch, the first thing people see.
Use this section to clearly communicate what you do and how you help. Keep it snappy, benefit-focused, and include a strong call-to-action (CTA). What’s the one thing you want your visitor to do first? Tell them here.

2. Trust Builders

Don’t be shy! This is where you put your best foot forward. You’re awesome and you need to show it off.
Include trust-building elements like:

  • Client logos
  • Awards
  • Certifications
  • 5-star review counts

This section is all about proving you’re legit and worth their time.

3. About / Why Choose Us

Your customers want to know who they’re working with.
This section builds connection and rapport. Share what makes you different, your story, your values, or even a quick intro video. Make it human and relatable.

4. Services or Products

Now that they know who you are, show them what you offer.
This is your chance to highlight your top services or bestselling products. Keep it visual, scannable, and easy to understand.

5. Social Proof – Don’t Just Say It, Display It

You’ve told them what you offer… now prove it!
Showcase:

  • Testimonials
  • Google reviews
  • Case studies
  • Before-and-afters
  • Client results

People want to know if you can actually deliver, and this is how you show them you can.

6. Benefits or How It Works

Help your visitors imagine what it’s like to work with you.
This section is all about making your process feel approachable and aligned with their goals. Whether it’s a “How It Works” walkthrough or a list of benefits, make it easy for them to say, “Yes, this is for me.”

Pro tip: Not everyone should convert. You want the right people to take action, the ones who are the best fit for you.

7. FAQ

Even after reading everything, visitors still might have a few hesitations.
A short FAQ helps calm nerves and answers those final “but what about…” questions that might otherwise stop them from reaching out.

8. Final CTA

They made it all the way to the bottom don’t leave them hanging.
Wrap up with a clear, strong CTA that ties everything together. This is your last chance to convert a visitor into a lead, customer, or subscriber. Don’t forget it.

Wrap-Up

And that’s my home page winning formula.
If you’re missing any of these sections, your visitors might be slipping away before they even get to know how awesome your offer really is.

title: Is your website readable?
description: Here are my top tips for improving readability so your website works better for your audience and your business.
excerpt: We spend so much time and energy creating great content—so let’s make sure it’s easy for people to enjoy it! Improving readability is one of my biggest priorities as a web design…
content:
We spend so much time and energy creating great content—so let’s make sure it’s easy for people to enjoy it!

Improving readability is one of my biggest priorities as a web designer. I honestly believe people do read online content, as long as we make it easy for them. Here are my top tips for improving readability so your website works better for your audience and your business.

Why Readability Matters

  1. It makes your website look professional: A clear, organized site leaves a great first impression and builds trust.
  2. It lowers bounce rates: When visitors aren’t immediately overwhelmed by messy layouts or walls of text, they’re more likely to stay.
  3. It keeps people on your site longer: When content is easy to read, people stick around. That extra time on the page is a big win.
  4. It helps with SEO: All these improvements tell Google that your site is user-friendly, which can help boost your ranking.

So, it’s not just about making things look nice—readability plays a big role in how your website performs.

Tips for Standard Web Pages

1. Break Content into Sections

Think of each section as its own mini-story. Your H2s should guide the reader by breaking your content into topics that are easy to skim.

  • Use background colors: This is one of my favorite tricks! Alternate between darker backgrounds with white text, light-colored backgrounds, and plain white to visually separate sections. It keeps things interesting and makes your site look super polished.
  • Add padding to sections: Each section should have some breathing room. Adding 50px of padding on the top and bottom is my go-to—it’s simple but effective.

2. Give Your Text Room to Breathe

Text needs space to stand out, so don’t cram everything together!

  • Use margins: Headlines, body copy, and CTAs shouldn’t be so close they’re touching. Give each element some space (I usually go with a 25px margin at the bottom). Consistent spacing throughout your site gives it that professional, polished vibe.
  • Line height matters: Adjust the space between lines of text so it’s easy to follow. A good rule of thumb is to set line height to 150% of your font size (e.g., a 16px font would need a 24px line height).

3. Don’t Let Your Text Stretch Across the Screen

Have you ever tried to read something that spans the entire width of a screen? It’s the worst!

  • Keep lines short: Break content into columns that are ⅔ or ½ the page width. Ideally, aim for about 12 words per line. This makes it much easier for people to stay focused while reading.

4. Choose Readable Fonts

Playful fonts can add personality, but they’re best kept to headlines. When it comes to body text, stick with simple, easy-to-read fonts that don’t strain the eyes.

5. Use Strong Color Contrast

Contrast is key for making text stand out and easy to read, especially for people with visual impairments or when viewing your site on mobile devices.

  • Text vs. Background: Make sure there’s enough contrast between your text and its background. For example, light gray text on a white background or yellow text on a light background is a no-go. Black text on white, or white text on a dark background, works much better.
  • Highlight with Color: Use high-contrast colors to make important elements like CTAs or headlines pop without being overwhelming.

Check your color contrast using this website: https://coolors.co/contrast-checker

Strong contrast isn’t just about looks—it ensures everyone can read your content easily, no matter their device or environment.

Blog-Specific Tips

1. Narrow the Content Column

A common mistake with blogs is letting the line of text stretch too wide. I suggest max-width of 900px for your text column to keep it easy to read.

2. Use Images to Break Things Up

Images aren’t just pretty—they’re a great way to give readers a mental break and help explain what the content is about. Plus, they make your page more fun to look at!

3. Break Up Long Paragraphs

Big blocks of text can feel overwhelming. Instead, break them into smaller chunks or use bullet points to make your content easier to scan.

By focusing on readability, you’re not just improving how your website looks—you’re making it more useful, welcoming, and effective. Your visitors will thank you, and so will your analytics!

title: Anatomy of a High-Converting Hero
description: Master the art of a high-converting hero section with tips on messaging, layout, visuals, and CTAs to turn visitors into customers.
excerpt: What is a Hero? Your hero section is your website’s first impression—and let’s be real, first impressions matter. It’s that big, bold section at the top of your homepage, the…
content:
What is a Hero?

Your hero section is your website’s first impression—and let’s be real, first impressions matter. It’s that big, bold section at the top of your homepage, the first thing people see when they land on your site.

It’s usually very visual, but let’s not forget—the copy and other elements are just as important (if not more!). A solid hero grabs attention, clearly communicates what you do, and guides visitors toward action—whether that’s clicking, scrolling, or exploring further. It should be clear, engaging, and instantly impactful.

Step 1: Define Your Audience

Before designing an effective hero section, you need to know who you’re talking to. The hero isn’t about you—it’s about your customer.

Ask yourself:

  • Who is my ideal visitor?
  • What problem do they need solved?
  • What action do I want them to take?

Once you have a clear picture of your audience, you can craft messaging that speaks directly to them.

Step 2: Craft the Message That Hooks Them

Think of your hero messaging like an elevator pitch—you’ve only got a few seconds to make an impact, so make it count.

Here’s my go-to formula:

1. H1 Tag (Your Focus Keyword)

This one’s mostly for SEO, so let’s be honest—it’s not always the most captivating of text. That’s why I usually style it smaller so it doesn’t steal the spotlight.

2. Headline (The Hook)

This is the big, bold statement that tells people what you do and how you help—in as few words as possible. No vague, fluffy nonsense.

🚫 “Innovative Solutions for a Better Tomorrow” (What does this even mean?!)
✅ “Launch a Website That Converts—No Templates, Just Results” (Now we’re talking!)

3. Supporting Text

A short sentence or bullet points explaining key features or how your service works. Keep it concise and scannable.

Step 3: Make the CTA (Call-to-Action) Button Obvious

This is the button we want people to click—so don’t make them hunt for it.

  • Be Crystal Clear – Tell them exactly what to do (e.g., “Get Your Free Quote” instead of “Learn More”).
  • Use High Contrasting Colors – Make your CTA button stand out.
  • Design that supports it – Everything in your hero should support and guide attention to the CTA.

Step 4: Build Trust with Add-Ons

Once you’ve nailed the message and CTA, add elements that reinforce credibility, such as:

  • “Trusted by 100+ businesses”
  • Certification logos or awards
  • Client testimonials

These small touches can boost conversions by making visitors feel more confident in your offer.

Step 5: Pick the Right Visuals

Your visuals should support your message—not just look pretty. That’s why I recommend crafting the messaging first and choosing visuals that reinforce it.

This hero features a model looking towards the CTA and builds trust with logos that people recognize.

Best-Converting Layouts:

  1. Text on the Left, Image on the Right – We read left to right, so put the most important info first.
  2. Centered Layout – Great for bold, simple messaging.

Choosing the Right Imagery:

  • Match your brand’s vibe (colors, tone, and style).
  • Use models wearing your brand colors for a cohesive look.
  • Guide the eye toward the CTA (e.g., models looking at or pointing to the button).
  • Angle product shots to subtly direct attention to your call-to-action.

Common Hero Mistakes to Avoid

This hero is hard to read with the text overtop of their face and low contrast between the text and the background.

  • Text Covering Faces – People naturally focus on faces, so don’t place text over them.
  • Slow Load Times – Size your images correctly and use nextgen image formats and avoid heavy video backgrounds.
  • Poor Contrast – Always check readability with a contrast checker.
  • Too Much Clutter – Too many elements in a small space make it hard to read.

Final Thoughts

Your hero section isn’t just a pretty banner—it’s your chance to hook visitors and get them to take action. Keep it focused, user-friendly, and conversion-driven, and you’ll have a hero that works for you!

title: Website, Domain, and Email Hosting: What’s the Difference?
seoTitle: Website vs Domain vs Email Hosting
description: Learn the difference between domain, web, and email hosting—and why separating them boosts flexibility and security. Get expert tips from Leanne DigitalDesign.
excerpt: Domain Hosting Your domain (e.g. www.yourbusiness.com) is the memorable address people type into their browser to find you. Domain hosts—companies like GoDaddy, NameCheap, or…
content:
Domain Hosting

Your domain (e.g. www.yourbusiness.com) is the memorable address people type into their browser to find you. Domain hosts—companies like GoDaddy, NameCheap, or Hover—handle the registration, renewals, and DNS settings that map your domain to your web host.

You pay an annual fee (typically $20–$30 for a common .com), and as long as you keep it renewed, your address stays yours. Behind the scenes, you’ll manage nameservers or A records, which quietly tell the internet where your site lives.

Web Hosting

Your web host provides the actual space on a server where all of your website’s files—HTML, images, videos, databases—are stored and served to visitors. Think of it as the plot of land and the foundation under your digital “house.” When someone types in your domain, the web host delivers the content.

Hosting plans also often include basic management tools (a control panel), automated backups, and support for uptime monitoring. Without a reliable web host, your site could slow down, go offline, or fail to load correctly.

Email Hosting

Your email host runs your business mailbox (you@yourbusiness.com). Providers like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Zoho Mail manage everything from spam filtering and attachment limits to calendars and contact syncing. Setting it up involves adding MX records to your domain’s DNS so that all incoming mail is routed through their servers.

Professional email hosting not only keeps your personal inbox separate but also boosts deliverability and trust with customers.

Email Hosting

Register your domain at a registrar (GoDaddy, NameCheap).

Buy web hosting from a host (SiteGround, Bluehost, etc.) and update your domain’s DNS to point there.

Set up email hosting with a provider (Google Workspace, Microsoft or Zoho Mail) by adding the required MX records.

Once configured, typing your domain in a browser loads your site files, and sending mail to you@yourbusiness.com delivers to your new mailbox.

Why Keep Them Separate

Flexibility: You can switch web hosts or email providers without moving your domain.

Security: Different logins and platforms reduce the blast radius if one account is hacked.

Best-in-Class: Pick specialized providers for each service rather than settling for an all-in-one bundle that may underperform in one area.

Final Thoughts

  • Domain Hosting = your easy-to-remember web address
  • Web Hosting = the server space and foundation for your website files
  • Email Hosting = your professional mailbox and communication hub

You can bundle all three at a single company for simplicity—or mix and match to optimize cost, performance, and features. Either way, understanding these distinctions is the first step toward a stable, secure, and professional online presence.

title: 5 Easy SEO Fixes You Can Do Today on Your WordPress Site
description: Five WordPress SEO fixes you can do in about 30 minutes: install Yoast, write better titles and meta descriptions, fix headings, optimize images, and add internal links.
excerpt: SEO in 30 Minutes or Less (Seriously!) So, you’ve got your WordPress website up and running, but it’s not showing up on Google the way you want it to. Don’t stress — improving…
content:
SEO in 30 Minutes or Less (Seriously!)

So, you’ve got your WordPress website up and running, but it’s not showing up on Google the way you want it to. Don’t stress — improving your SEO doesn’t have to be complicated or time-consuming. With just a few simple steps, you can see better results in 30 minutes or less.

Ready to boost your website’s visibility on search engines? Let’s dive in!

Install Yoast SEO for a Simple SEO Solution

First things first, if you haven’t already, get Yoast SEO installed. This popular plugin is a game-changer when it comes to simplifying SEO for your WordPress site. Think of Yoast as your personal SEO assistant, guiding you through each page to make it more SEO-friendly. It’s like having a coach by your side, minus the expensive hourly rates!

Optimize Your SEO Titles and Meta Descriptions

Next up — SEO titles and meta descriptions. These are what show up in search engine results, and they play a huge role in attracting clicks. Keep them clear, concise, and focused on keywords relevant to your business.

  • SEO Title: This is the clickable title that shows up in search results. Be sure to include your main keyword.
  • Meta Description: This is the short snippet under the title in search results. It’s like your page’s elevator pitch. Include keywords, but don’t make it sound like a robot wrote it.

For example, if you own a bakery, your SEO title might be “Fresh, Handmade Breads | Bakery Name,” and your meta description could be “Visit Bakery Name for delicious, fresh breads baked daily. We offer gluten-free and vegan options too!” See how easy that is?

Check Your H1 Tag for Clarity and Keywords

Now, let’s talk about your H1 tag — this is the main title on your page, and it tells both users and search engines what your page is about. Make sure your H1 is clear and descriptive, and that it includes relevant keywords.

Don’t use something vague like “Welcome to My Website!” Google doesn’t care about that. For our bakery example, a better H1 would be “Fresh Baked Goods Every Day at Bakery Name.”

Remember: Only one H1 tag per page is needed — that’s the gold standard!

Use H2 and H3 Tags to Organize Content

Once your H1 is set, it’s time to structure the rest of your content with H2 and H3 tags. These subheadings make it easier for both your visitors and search engines to navigate your page.

Start with H2s for main sections (like “Our Signature Breads” or “Gluten-Free Options”) and use H3s for further details. Proper hierarchy is key: H1 for your main title, H2 for sections, and H3 for sub-sections. This helps Google understand your page’s structure.

Optimize Your Images for Speed and SEO

It’s easy to forget about images, but they can have a major impact on your site’s performance. Big, slow images can drag your site’s speed down — and search engines like Google hate slow sites.

Here’s how to optimize your images:

  • Rename images to something descriptive and keyword-rich (e.g., “fresh-sourdough-bread.jpg”).
  • Resize your images to keep file sizes under 200KB. Faster images = faster site.
  • Use the right format: Stick with .jpg or .webp for most images, and use .png only for images with transparent backgrounds.

Also, make sure your images have proper alt text. It’s not only good for accessibility, but it also gives Google a better understanding of your images.

Add Internal Links to Boost SEO and User Experience

Internal links are an underrated, but powerful, SEO tool. By linking to other pages on your website, you help Google understand the structure of your site. Plus, it makes it easier for visitors to explore related content.

For example, on your bakery’s homepage, you could link to a page on “gluten-free bread options” or “custom cakes for events.” Just make sure the links are relevant and useful to your readers.

Final Thoughts

Improving your SEO doesn’t have to be a daunting task. With just a few simple changes — like installing Yoast, optimizing titles and descriptions, and using the right headings — you’ll start to see a difference in how your site performs on search engines.

And remember, SEO is an ongoing process. Keep tweaking, updating, and improving as you go. In 30 minutes, you can make a huge impact, and with a little time, your WordPress site will be ranking higher and driving more traffic.
